situation: A teammate's 400-line service method handles validation, pricing and notifications, and you have to add a new discount rule to it before Friday.

options.text: Add the rule with a few more if-statements inside the method. The deadline matters most.
Add the rule as is, and leave a TODO to clean the method up another day.
Pull the pricing logic into its own well-named unit with tests, then add the rule there.
Introduce a small pricing-rule abstraction so new discounts plug in, migrate the existing rules behind tests, and agree the direction with the team in the PR.

situation: You change a payment-retry function that calls a third-party gateway. The existing tests are slow and sometimes fail because they hit the real sandbox.

options.text: Skip automated tests for this change and verify it manually in staging.
Re-run the flaky tests until they pass, then merge.
Stub the gateway client in unit tests covering success, timeout and duplicate responses, and keep the sandbox for a few integration tests.
Do that, then add contract tests against the gateway's schema and share the stub so other services stop hitting the sandbox.

situation: An orders list screen got slow after the table grew to 50 million rows. The query filters by user_id and status and sorts by created_at.

options.text: Ask for a bigger database instance.
Add a separate index on each filtered column.
Check the query plan, add a composite index that matches the filter and sort order, and confirm the plan changes.
Do that, then weigh keyset pagination or archiving old rows, and measure the write cost of the new index before rollout.

situation: Your service calls a partner API that has started timing out under load, and your threads are piling up.

options.text: Increase the timeout and the thread pool size.
Add a retry on every failure.
Set tight timeouts, retry idempotent calls with backoff and jitter, and add a circuit breaker with a fallback.
Do that, isolate this dependency with bulkheads so it can't starve other traffic, alert on breaker state, and agree degraded behaviour with product and the partner.

situation: At 2 a.m. you are paged: the error rate on checkout jumped from 0.2% to 6%. A deploy went out 20 minutes ago.

options.text: Wait and see if it settles, and look again in the morning.
Restart the service and see whether the errors go away.
Check the dashboard and logs for the failing endpoint, correlate with the deploy, and roll back if the deploy is the likely cause.
Roll back first to stop the impact, then isolate the cause with traces and logs, write a timeline, and file follow-ups for the detection gap.

situation: You find a payment provider API key hardcoded in a repository that several teams can read.

options.text: Leave it. The repository is internal.
Move it to an environment variable in a new commit.
Rotate the key straight away, move it to the secrets manager, and remove it from the code.
Rotate it, move it to the secrets manager, scrub it from history, add secret scanning to CI, and check access logs for misuse.

situation: You use an AI coding assistant to generate a data-migration script for customer records.

options.text: Run it on production because the output looks right.
Skim it and run it on staging.
Review it line by line, test it on a copy of the data with edge cases, and keep real customer data out of the prompts.
Do that, write the constraints into the prompt, add tests the AI didn't write, and document the prompt so teammates can reuse it safely.

situation: Product asks for in-app notifications for 6 different events, with more expected next quarter.

options.text: Write six separate code paths, one per event.
Build the first one, then copy it and tweak it for each event.
Define a common event and handler interface, implement the six handlers behind it, and keep delivery decoupled.
Do that, write a short design doc covering failure modes and scale, and review it with peers before building.

situation: A screen's controller has grown to 1,500 lines mixing networking, formatting and UI logic, and you need to add a new card type to it.

options.text: Add the card type in the same file.
Add it and move a couple of helper functions out.
Move the logic behind a presenter or view-model with tests, then add the card type through it.
Propose a screen architecture pattern, migrate this screen as the template, and document it for the team.

situation: Users report the app drains battery and that a long feed stutters on mid-range phones.

options.text: Tell users to close background apps.
Shrink the images wherever you happen to notice jank.
Profile with the platform tools, find main-thread work and leaks, fix the top offenders, and compare before and after.
Do that, set performance budgets with automated regression checks in CI, and track them with production metrics.

situation: A release build is found logging auth tokens and the API base URL in plain text.

options.text: Ignore it. Users can't see the logs.
Remove the token logging in the next release.
Strip sensitive logging from release builds, keep tokens in the keystore or keychain, and rotate any exposed tokens.
Do that, add a CI lint for sensitive logging, enable obfuscation or pinning where justified, and review other local data stores.

situation: The order screen fails when the network drops mid-request, and some users end up with duplicate orders.

options.text: Show a generic error and let users tap retry.
Retry automatically on every failure.
Use idempotency keys, retry with backoff, and show clear offline and error states.
Do that, design the queue and sync behaviour with the backend team, and test flaky-network cases systematically.

situation: Crash-free sessions dropped from 99.6% to 98.1% after the latest release.

options.text: Wait for more user reports before doing anything.
Look at the top crash in the dashboard and guess at a fix.
Group crashes by version, device and OS, find the main cause from the stack traces, and ship a fix or halt the rollout.
Halt the staged rollout, fix the cause, add the case to tests, and tune alerting so it is caught at 1% rollout next time.

situation: The release build fails on CI but works locally, one day before a store submission.

options.text: Submit the binary you built locally.
Re-run CI and hope it passes.
Compare the two environments and logs, find the difference in signing, config or dependency version, and fix CI.
Fix it, pin the toolchain versions, and automate signing and store release so it can't recur.

situation: You receive a PRD for a new wallet top-up flow two days before release. Some edge cases are not specified.

options.text: Test only the happy path described in the PRD.
Run the standard test cases and report pass or fail.
Derive cases from the PRD including edge cases, ask the PM about the unspecified behaviour, and test those too.
Do that, risk-rank the scenarios, assess regression impact, and agree with the team what ships and what is deferred.

situation: A new API returns 200 with an empty body when the user is not authorised.

options.text: Mark it as passed because the status is 200.
Raise a bug saying the response is empty.
Raise a bug explaining the auth contract is violated (expect 401 or 403), with the request, response and repro in Postman.
Do that, add negative auth cases to the automated suite, and check other endpoints for the same pattern.

situation: You find a bug that happens about one time in ten on checkout.

options.text: Mention it informally. It's hard to reproduce.
Raise a ticket saying checkout sometimes fails.
Raise a ticket with steps, data, environment, frequency, logs and a screen recording.
Do that, narrow down the trigger conditions, link related defects, and flag severity and release impact to the owner.

situation: A release has 120 test cases, a 2-day window and a team of two.

options.text: Run what you can and skip the rest.
Split the cases equally and run them in order.
Prioritise by risk and recent change, automate the repeatable checks, and agree what is out of scope.
Do that, use defect history to refine priorities, and set a roadmap to move high-value regression into automation.

situation: A production deployment completes and the pipeline status is green.

options.text: Close the ticket.
Check that the app opens.
Run deployment verification: key flows, health endpoints and error rates.
Do that, and turn the verification into an automated pipeline gate with rollback criteria.

situation: A developer disputes your bug and says it is expected behaviour.

options.text: Reopen the ticket repeatedly until it is fixed.
Escalate it to your manager.
Share your evidence and the spec reference, and talk it through together to agree on expected behaviour.
Do that, and get the PRD clarified so the ambiguity doesn't come back on future work.

situation: A customer reports their ride booking is stuck, but the support dashboards show no error.

options.text: Ask the customer to try again later.
Escalate to engineering with the ticket as it is.
Pull the logs for the booking ID, follow the flow across services, and find where it stalled.
Do that, identify the root cause, document the steps in the runbook, and propose an alert for it.

situation: You need to check whether an internal API returns the right fields for a user.

options.text: Ask a developer to check for you.
Use a saved Postman request someone else made.
Call it from Postman or curl with the right method, headers and auth, and validate the response.
Do that, and turn it into a reusable collection with environments for the rest of the team.

situation: A customer escalates angrily about a delayed refund. The delay is on the bank's side.

options.text: Tell them it isn't your fault.
Say you will look into it.
Acknowledge the problem, explain the status and timeline clearly, and follow up when it is closed.
Do that, record the root cause, and flag the pattern so proactive messaging can be added.

situation: You need the number of failed payments per day over the last week.

options.text: Ask engineering for the number.
Select all rows and count them by hand.
Write a grouped SQL query with a date filter on the right table.
Do that, check index use and limits so it is safe on production, and save it as a reusable report.

situation: A daily revenue dashboard shows a 30% drop, but operations says trip volume is normal.

options.text: Tell stakeholders the data is what it is.
Re-run the pipeline.
Trace the lineage to find the break (a missing partition, schema change or dropped duplicates), fix it and backfill.
Do that, then add automated freshness, volume and schema checks so it is caught before the dashboard.

situation: A nightly pipeline fails halfway through a load. It is re-run, and now the target has duplicates.

options.text: Delete the duplicate rows by hand each time.
Add a clean-up step after the load.
Make the load idempotent with a merge or partition overwrite, and add retries.
Do that, add orchestration alerts and backfill tooling, and agree SLAs with the consumers.

situation: Analysts need to slice trips by city, vehicle type and time, and the source systems change often.

options.text: Give them the raw tables.
Build one wide table with everything in it.
Model facts and dimensions around the business process, with keys and documented definitions.
Do that, handle slowly changing dimensions and versioned definitions, and align the model with the data architecture.

situation: You have built a new pipeline and want to release it.

options.text: Run it manually in production.
Test it locally and deploy it by hand.
Ship it through CI/CD with tests, staging validation and a rollback plan.
Do that, with infrastructure as code, monitoring and cost controls built in.

situation: Product wants to commit 5 large items this quarter. Your team's capacity covers about 3.

options.text: Agree to all five and hope the team stretches.
Tell product the team can't do it.
Use capacity data to show the trade-off, rank by business impact, and agree what is committed and what is stretch.
Do that, surface cross-team dependencies early, and revisit the plan monthly with your leads.

situation: Sprint spillover has been above 30% for three sprints in a row.

options.text: Ask the team to work harder.
Remind the team about estimates in the retro.
Analyse the causes (scope churn, estimates, blockers), agree specific changes in planning, and track the trend.
Do that, and resolve cross-team dependency causes together with the other managers.

situation: A major incident last week was caused by a missing alert, and a similar one happened last quarter.

options.text: Close the incident.
Add the missing alert.
Run a blameless RCA, track the action items to closure, and review whether it recurs.
Do that, look for the pattern across incidents, and set reliability standards for the wider org.

situation: Two senior engineers disagree about build versus buy for a notification service.

options.text: Back whoever argues best in the meeting.
Let them settle it between themselves and stay out of it.
Frame the criteria (cost, time, risk, maintainability), review the options, and decide with the reasoning documented.
Do that, involve the key stakeholders, and set checkpoints so the decision can be reversed if needed.

situation: A strong engineer's output has dropped over the past two months.

options.text: Wait for the performance review cycle.
Ask in stand-up whether everything is fine.
Hold a 1:1 to understand what is going on, give specific feedback, and agree actions.
Do that, check workload and team factors that may be contributing, and follow up regularly with a development plan.

situation: Your engagement score fell sharply and two engineers hint they are interviewing elsewhere.

options.text: Ignore it. Some attrition is normal.
Announce to the team that you are open to feedback.
Talk to each person, learn what is driving it (workload, growth), and commit to visible actions.
Do that, take systemic causes to leadership, and track engagement over time.
